# My grooming van nearly caught fire. Here’s what happened, and what I wish I’d asked before it was built.

Last Wednesday, October 28, at about 2:15 in the afternoon, I was in a client’s driveway in Bedford, drying a Bernese mountain dog called Moose.

The dryer was on high. Moose was being Moose. It was a normal working afternoon, right up until I smelled hot plastic.

At first I thought it was the dryer motor.

Then I saw smoke coming out from under the bench seat where my batteries are.

I turned off the battery switch, got Moose out through the side door, and used a bit of the fire extinguisher. I’m still not sure whether the extinguisher was needed. In the moment, I wasn’t interested in waiting to find out.

Moose was still damp and absolutely delighted to have his groom interrupted by an unexpected outdoor adventure.

I was shaking.

His mum brought me a coffee and sat with me on her front steps. That kindness is one of the things I remember most clearly, along with the smell.

Everyone is okay. Nobody was hurt. That is the important part.

But my van is off the road for at least three weeks, I’ve cancelled 31 appointments so far, and the repair quote is $4,200. My whole income comes out of that van. Rent is still due on the first.

I’m writing this partly because I need to explain what’s happening, and partly because another groomer I know is about to put down a deposit with the same builder.

Tasha, please get the electrical details in writing before you send any money.

And for the other groomer girls reading this: please don’t assume that because your van looks tidy, the electrical work underneath is right.

I did.

## First: I am not an electrician

I’m a dog groomer. I’m not qualified to design, inspect or repair a high-current battery system, and this post is not a guide to rewiring your own van.

The electrical explanations here are my understanding of what Priya, from Sackville Marine Electric, showed me after the incident. Where I’ve included calculations, I’ve kept the assumptions visible, because I don’t want to replace one bad assumption with another.

If something in your van worries you, get a qualified electrician with experience in battery-and-inverter installations to look at it.

Not someone who says they’ve “done loads of vans.” Someone who can explain the design, show you the specifications and check the actual installation.

Also, if you smell burning or see smoke, that is not the time to get your thermometer out and investigate. Get yourself, the dog and anyone else out. Call 911 if there’s smoke, fire or any doubt about safety. Don’t go back into a smoking van to reach a switch.

I was able to switch mine off. Please don’t take my particular sequence of events as instructions for yours.

## What was installed in my van

My conversion was built by Coastline Van Fitouts, through Darren, in spring 2025.

The relevant bits of the electrical setup were:

- A 3,000-watt inverter.
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries in a 12-volt system.
- A 4 AWG cable running from the battery supply to the inverter.
- A 300-amp ANL fuse, mounted approximately 90 centimetres from the battery.

The damage was at the positive cable lug. That’s the metal terminal fitted onto the end of the cable.

The lug was blackened, and the cable’s insulation had melted back by about three centimetres.

Priya identified the cable sizing, the positive connection and the fuse arrangement as things that needed addressing. Her repair quote includes rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and a Class T fuse.

I’ve sent Darren three texts and an email and haven’t had a response as I write this.

I’m naming the business because who built the installation is relevant, especially to people currently choosing a builder. I’m not going to guess what Darren knew, what tools he used or why it was done this way. I can describe what happened in my van and what the electrician found.

## The bit I hadn’t understood: 12 volts means a lot of current

I knew my dryer was a big electrical load.

What I hadn’t properly understood was how much current the batteries have to supply to run it through an inverter.

My dryer draws roughly 1,800–2,000 watts. The simple calculation is:

**Current in amps = power in watts ÷ voltage.**

At a nominal 12 volts, that works out to:

- 1,800 watts ÷ 12 volts = **150 amps**.
- 2,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = **about 167 amps**.

But that is the simplified version. An inverter isn’t perfectly efficient. Some energy is lost in the conversion from battery power to the power the dryer uses.

If we use 90% inverter efficiency as an example—not a measurement of my particular inverter—the battery-side current becomes:

- 1,800 watts ÷ (12 volts × 0.90) = **about 167 amps**.
- 2,000 watts ÷ (12 volts × 0.90) = **about 185 amps**.

That’s just the dryer.

The water heater sometimes runs too. Additional loads increase the total demand, but I don’t have a confirmed heater wattage or a record of exactly what was running at that moment, so I’m not going to invent a precise current for the incident.

The figure I originally scribbled down was “150–250 amps.” That describes the sort of current we were discussing, not a reading anyone took while the cable was smoking.

For another point of reference, supplying a full 3,000 watts at 12 volts would mean **250 amps before allowing for inverter losses**, or about **278 amps at 90% efficiency**. Current also changes with the actual battery voltage.

The inverter doesn’t draw its full rated power constantly just because “3,000W” is printed on it. The load matters. But the wiring has to be designed properly for what the system can be asked to do.

Those numbers made the cable under my bench feel a lot less like an ordinary wire and a lot more like something I should have asked questions about.

## The cable was too small for the installation Priya assessed

The battery-to-inverter cable in my van was 4 AWG.

Priya told me that, for my 3,000-watt, 12-volt installation, it should have been 2/0 AWG.

For anyone else who doesn’t spend their evenings reading cable charts: **2/0 is substantially larger than 4 AWG**. The naming is not especially helpful to those of us encountering it after a small crisis.

I do need to be careful here. “Every 3,000-watt inverter needs exactly this cable” is not a rule I’m qualified to give you.

Cable selection depends on the inverter manufacturer’s requirements, the length of the cable run, the cable and insulation ratings, how it is routed, temperature, voltage drop and other installation details. Both the positive and negative sides matter.

The useful takeaway is not to order whatever cable I mention in a blog post.

It is to ask your builder or electrician:

**What cable size is specified for this inverter, at this voltage, over this distance—and does the installed cable match that design?**

I never asked that.

I saw a tidy conversion and assumed someone had already worked it out.

## The connection mattered too

The other thing Priya showed me was the positive cable lug.

Her assessment was that it had not been properly crimped. To my eyes, it looked like it had been squeezed or hammered rather than finished with the correct crimping equipment. I didn’t watch it being made, so I can’t say what tool was actually used.

The connection had been covered with heat-shrink tubing.

From the outside, that helped it look finished. It didn’t tell me whether the connection underneath was sound.

My understanding of Priya’s explanation is that a poor connection can add resistance at a very small point. When a large current passes through that point, it can generate a lot of heat.

The relationship is **heat generated = current squared × resistance**.

I don’t need to pretend I could design a system from that equation to understand why a bad connection carrying hundreds of amps is a serious problem.

This is also why “the cable was too small” isn’t the whole story. The cable, the terminals, the quality of the crimps, the connections and the protective devices all have to work together.

I can tell you where the visible damage was and what Priya identified. I can’t separate out exactly how much each problem contributed to the overheating. That would be claiming more than I know.

What I do know is that the positive lug was black and the insulation beside it had melted.

## Why didn’t the fuse stop it?

This was one of my first questions.

There was a fuse. Surely that was supposed to stop something like this?

Apparently, having a fuse is not the same as having protection against every way an installation can overheat.

A fuse responds to current according to its rating and operating characteristics. A bad connection can become dangerously hot without the total current being high enough, for long enough, to make that fuse open.

So a fuse that hasn’t blown does **not** prove everything downstream is safe.

There was also the question of its location.

My 300A ANL fuse was approximately 90 centimetres from the battery. Priya said she wanted the protection much closer—around 18 centimetres for the arrangement we were discussing.

The reason, as I understand it, is that the stretch of positive cable between the battery and that fuse isn’t protected by that fuse if it shorts to the van’s metalwork.

I’m not presenting 18 centimetres as a universal legal limit for every van. The applicable requirements and any permitted exceptions need checking by someone qualified. But “close to the battery” is not a cosmetic preference. There’s a reason for it.

The fuse rating also has to suit the cable and the system. A big number on a fuse is not automatically a good thing.

Priya’s repair specification includes a Class T fuse. One reason fuse type matters with lithium batteries is that the protection needs to be capable of safely interrupting the very high fault current the batteries may be able to supply.

I’m not telling everyone with an ANL fuse to swap it themselves. Please have a professional check the fuse type, rating, interrupting capacity, holder and placement against your actual batteries and installation.

## Tidy is not the same as right

This is the sentence I keep coming back to.

**Tidy is not the same as right.**

My van looked finished. The batteries were tucked away. The cables had coverings. The fittings looked neat.

I took that as reassurance about things I couldn’t see and didn’t understand.

Priya pulled up my damage photos next to thermal-camera images of her own van running a similar kind of load. In hers, the corresponding wiring barely warmed in comparison.

Seeing those side by side was horrible.

They weren’t identical systems being tested in a laboratory, and a thermal image on its own doesn’t certify an installation. But it made the difference very real to me.

Mine had not just been experiencing some inevitable amount of “working hard.”

Something was wrong.

## A power-off checklist that doesn’t involve taking your van apart

I wanted something practical to put here, because “get it checked” is important but can feel vague.

This is a **visual and paperwork checklist**, not an electrical inspection. Passing it does not mean your van is safe.

Before looking around, shut down your equipment and follow the proper shutdown procedure for your installation. Disconnect shore power where applicable.

And please understand this bit: **turning off an inverter or battery switch does not necessarily make every cable dead**. Batteries, solar panels, chargers and other supplies can leave parts energised.

Don’t remove electrical covers, touch terminals, disconnect cables, tighten anything or peel back heat-shrink. If you don’t know what’s safe to access, leave it alone.

From areas you can normally see without dismantling anything:

### 1. Look and smell for changes

Any lingering burnt-plastic smell? Discolouration? Melted insulation? Scorch marks? A cable covering that has changed shape?

If yes, don’t power it back up to “see if it still does it.” Arrange a professional inspection.

### 2. Look for visible cable damage

Check accessible cable routes for rubbing against sharp edges, trapped insulation or places where normal storage could crush or knock wiring.

Don’t move a heavy battery or pull a cable out to get a better look.

### 3. Check what lives beside the electrical equipment

Could bottles leak onto it? Could tools or loose metal fall near exposed electrical parts? Is equipment being buried under towels or other stored items?

Keep the space clear in line with the equipment’s installation requirements. Don’t assume that a bench enclosure can be packed full just because there’s room.

### 4. Find your documentation

Do you have the inverter model, battery models, wiring diagram, cable sizes and fuse specifications?

If not, ask for them. A photograph of a tidy cupboard is not a wiring diagram.

### 5. Identify your shutdown controls

Do you know where the normal isolators are and what each one disconnects?

Could you explain them to someone covering your appointments? Are they labelled?

Ask the electrician to explain what can remain live after shutdown, too.

### 6. Check your detection and emergency arrangements

I had no smoke detector in the rear workspace—just the one in the cab that came with the van.

I’m having suitable detection and placement addressed before I go back to work. I won’t be assuming the cab detector adequately covers a separate working area.

Check your extinguisher’s condition and service information, and get advice about suitable equipment and placement. Know your exits. Keep them usable.

### 7. Book the actual electrical check

Ask for the main battery cables, connections, protection, routing and equipment requirements to be assessed, including under an appropriate controlled load if the professional considers that safe.

There are problems you cannot find by looking at insulation from the outside.

Mine was one of them.

## About the $40 infrared thermometer

I bought an infrared thermometer for about $40 at Canadian Tire.

I wish I’d thought about temperature before I smelled melted plastic, and I think an inexpensive thermometer can be useful for noticing changes in accessible surfaces during otherwise normal operation.

But it is not a safety certificate.

It reads surface temperature, not the hidden connection under heat-shrink. Shiny metal can give misleading readings. Where you point it, the distance and the surface all affect what it tells you.

Please don’t open electrical compartments or deliberately run a suspect installation at high load to do your own heat test. If something smells hot, looks damaged or seems abnormal, shut down safely and get help.

There isn’t one magic temperature I can give you that makes every cable and connection safe.

The thermometer is an extra observation tool. It is not a substitute for properly sized cables, sound connections or an electrician.

## Before you pay a builder a deposit

Tasha, this is the bit I most want you to read.

Ask for the electrical specifications **in writing before the deposit**, including:

- The proposed inverter and battery models.
- The loads the system is designed to run together.
- Main positive and negative cable sizes and run lengths.
- Main fuse type, rating and location.
- How the protection has been selected for the batteries and cables.
- Who will carry out and verify the electrical work.
- What testing and documentation you will receive at handover.

Ask how the design follows the equipment manufacturers’ installation instructions and the requirements applicable to your van.

If the answer is “don’t worry, we always do it this way,” keep asking.

And if you’re spending your savings on a vehicle that will be your workplace and your income, consider paying for an independent electrical inspection before final handover.

I wish I had.

It wouldn’t have made me difficult. It would have made me someone checking the part of the build I wasn’t qualified to judge myself.

## Where things stand now

The repair quote is $4,200. That covers rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and Class T protection.

Parts are on order. I’m looking at a minimum of three weeks off the road.

I’ve cancelled 31 appointments so far. If yours is one of them, I’m sorry. I know people plan around these appointments, and I hate letting you down. But I’m not putting a dog back in that van until the electrical work has been repaired and checked.

Insurance is still a “maybe.” The adjuster is due Thursday, and I don’t yet know what will be covered.

Darren hasn’t replied to my three texts and email. If I receive a response, I’ll include the relevant information in an update.

Mostly, I’m relieved and scared at the same time.

I’m grateful Moose is fine. I’m grateful his mum sat with me while I shook. I’m also staring at the calendar, counting missed appointments and trying to work out how to pay for repairs while the thing that earns the money is waiting for parts.

I don’t have a cheerful ending to put on that yet.

Please ask the awkward questions about your van. Get the cable sizes and fuse specifications. Have someone qualified look beyond the tidy finish.

I’ll post again when mine is repaired and back on the road.

And Moose: sorry about the damp exit. You handled the afternoon considerably better than I did.
